terms.definition: An object that says which field to sort by and whether the order goes up or down.
terms.example: Use an NSSortDescriptor to show the newest note first.
terms.code:
import Foundation
let d = NSSortDescriptor(
    key: "title", ascending: false)
print(d.key ?? "none")
print(d.ascending)

terms.definition: A link from one stored object to another, such as a folder that holds many notes.
terms.example: Each folder has a relationship to its notes.
terms.code:
import CoreData
let rel = NSRelationshipDescription()
rel.name = "notes"
rel.maxCount = 0
print(rel.isToMany)

terms.definition: A setting that says what happens to the linked objects when you delete one object.
terms.example: Set the delete rule to cascade, so the notes go with the folder.
terms.code:
import CoreData
let rel = NSRelationshipDescription()
rel.deleteRule = .cascadeDeleteRule
print(rel.deleteRule == .cascadeDeleteRule)

dialogue.title: Folders and notes

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Jake, the notes in each folder look random. How do I sort them?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Use an NSSortDescriptor, like `s` in our code. It picks the field and the direction.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So `ascending: false` puts the newest note first?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes, if the key is `date`. The NSSortDescriptor sorts by that field.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Now I want each folder to hold many notes.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That is a relationship. It links one folder object to many note objects.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: What happens to the notes if I delete the folder?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That depends on the delete rule.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Oh. I thought Core Data always deleted them.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: No, a wrong delete rule can leave orphan notes. Here, `cascadeDeleteRule` removes them with the folder.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So the relationship needs a delete rule on purpose.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Exactly. Choose it carefully, and add an NSSortDescriptor for the list.
